newsitem.title: USA: Clinton veto marks symbolic shift in U.S. power.
newsitem.headline: Clinton veto marks symbolic shift in U.S. power.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's use of the line-item veto on Monday marked a symbolic shift of Washington's power levers from Congress to the White House.
The line-item veto gives the president the authority to strike out parts of spending bills and narrowly targeted tax breaks in the age-old fight to slice pork from the budget.

A long line of presidents had wanted it, going back well over a century. The Repubican-controlled Congress made it part of their legislative agenda and approved it last year even though a Democrat held the White House.
Critics believe it is unconstitutional, that it takes away from Congress its sacrosanct power as the final voice over spending decisions. It will doubtless face legal challenges.
Its proponents insist it gives back to the president an executive branch check on legislative excess.
Clinton said in exercising it for the first time that he he would use the line-item veto against "the most egregious" cases of pork-barrel spending.
That represents a profound change in the way spending decisions are made in Washington.
In the past, members of Congress would tack on to major budget legislation some individual items that would benefit few constituents -- money for a new bridge, or subsidies for mohair producers.

The president would reluctantly go along with them rather than veto the whole bill in protest, because it was not worth making a fight over $1 million here and $1 million there out of a $1.7 trillion budget.
Now, he has the power to use the line-item authority to advance his own agenda, if he wants.

"Its impact on the deficit is small but it gives the president a real sledgehammer to use against Congress to say, you vote how I want or you put in the money I want or this little project in your state is gone," said budget analyst Stan Collender of Burson-Marsteller.

Congress has 30 days to vote to disapprove of Clinton's decision. He would then presumably issue another veto, which would force Congress to try to override Clinton's decision with a two-thirds majority vote. White House aides consider Congress unlikely to take the fight that far.
Out of America's 50 states, 43 governors have the same authority. Clinton had it while governor of Arkansas.
He said he hopes the mere knowledge that the line-item veto exists will lead members of Congress to restrain themselves from budget abuses.
